column1: -3300000|c. 3.3 million years ago|Kenya|Lomekwi|Stone before written memory|Flakes and cores at Lomekwi preserve deliberate stone-working. They do not identify who struck them. At this scale a date marks a layer of sediment, not a calendar year.

-1800000|c. 1.8 million years ago|Georgia|Dmanisi hominins|Early humans outside Africa|Skulls and stone tools at Dmanisi preserve a population living in the Caucasus. Researchers disagree about how many species the strikingly different skull shapes represent.

-300000|c. 300,000 years ago|Africa|Homo sapiens|The emergence of our species|Fossils and genetics place the emergence of Homo sapiens in Africa. Different features appeared at different times and places. A single birthplace or birthday would imply precision the evidence cannot supply.

-70000|Tens of thousands of years ago|Southern Africa|Blombos Cave|Making marks that survive|Engraved ochre and pierced shells survive in cave deposits. Their makers left a pattern we can study, but no explanation of its meaning.

-50000|At least 50,000 years ago|Australia and New Guinea|Prehistory of Australia|People reach Sahul|Crossing stretches of open water brought people to the landmass that once joined Australia and New Guinea. Archaeology and Aboriginal traditions preserve different kinds of knowledge. The earliest arrival date remains debated.

-21000|c. 23,000–21,000 years ago|North America|White Sands National Park|Footsteps at an Ice Age lake|Footprints in New Mexico challenge a late peopling of the Americas. Initial dates depended on aquatic seeds that might carry old carbon. Pollen and sediment dating supplied independent checks. The prints alone cannot tell us which route their makers took.

-15000|Late Ice Age|Western Europe|Lascaux|Painting by lamplight|Artists painted animals deep inside a cave where natural light did not reach. The images survive. Hunting rituals, storytelling and other proposed purposes are interpretations.

-10000|c. 10,000 BCE onwards|Southwest Asia|Neolithic Revolution|Growing food changes daily life|Communities increasingly tended plants and animals. Farming also arose independently elsewhere. Dependence on fewer crops could bring hunger and disease alongside larger settlements.

-9600|From c. 9600 BCE|Anatolia|Göbekli Tepe|Building together before cities|People carved and raised monumental pillars. Calling the site a temple gives one interpretation of its use. Evidence of domestic activity complicates a simple division between sacred and everyday space.

-8000|Early Holocene|East Asia|History of rice cultivation|Wetlands become fields|Plant remains and changing grain traits help trace rice cultivation in the Yangtze basin. Tending wild stands and domesticating a crop were stages across many generations.

-7000|From c. 7000 BCE|New Guinea|Kuk Swamp|Gardening in the highlands|Traces of drainage and cultivated plants preserve the work of early farmers. Organic tools perish and their absence can make a cultivated landscape look unoccupied.

-6500|Seventh millennium BCE|Anatolia|Çatalhöyük|A settlement entered through rooftops|Walls, ovens and burials under house floors preserve the texture of domestic life. Unequal grave goods can suggest differences in status without revealing exactly how power worked.

-5000|Fifth millennium BCE|Southeast Europe|Varna Necropolis|Wealth enters the grave|Graves at Varna contain strikingly unequal amounts of gold. The objects provide evidence about burial practice. Reconstructing the social position of each person is more difficult.

-3500|Fourth millennium BCE|Mesopotamia|Uruk|Feeding and recording a city|Urban households, workshops and institutions exchanged food and labour on a new scale. Accounting tablets illuminate what administrators counted and leave much of ordinary life unwritten.

-3200|c. 3200 BCE|Nile Valley|Egyptian hieroglyphs|Words outlive their speakers|Early inscriptions recorded names, goods and authority. Written evidence is selective from its first appearance: people with access to scribes are easier to hear.

-3000|Third millennium BCE|Peru|Caral–Supe civilization|Cities on the Peruvian coast|Communities built monumental platforms and gathered in sunken plazas. Coastal fishing and inland farming connected households across different environments.

-2600|c. 2600–1900 BCE|South Asia|Indus Valley Civilisation|Planned cities with unread signs|Drains, streets, weights and seals illuminate urban life. Readers have proposed several languages for the Indus signs. No decipherment has achieved scholarly consensus.

-2300|Third millennium BCE|Mesopotamia|Akkadian Empire|An empire in its own words|Royal inscriptions celebrated conquest. Archaeology and local records complicate accounts written to glorify rulers and justify their power.

-1600|Second millennium BCE|East Asia|Shang dynasty|Questions preserved on bone|Shang diviners inscribed questions about crops, warfare and childbirth on bone and shell. Their records make the concerns of one court unusually visible.

-1500|Second millennium BCE|Pacific|Lapita culture|Sailing between islands|Distinctive pottery and settlement sites trace expanding networks across the Pacific. Languages and genetics offer complementary evidence about movement and exchange.

-1200|Around 1200 BCE|Eastern Mediterranean|Late Bronze Age collapse|When palace economies failed|Destruction layers mark the end of some centres while others survived. Drought, conflict, migration and trade disruption explain different parts of the pattern. No single cause fits every site.

-1000|First millennium BCE|West Africa|Nok culture|Faces modelled in clay|Nok terracottas preserve skilled work and distinctive artistic choices. Looting removes objects from their original layers and destroys evidence needed to interpret them.

-600|First millennium BCE|Central America|Maya civilization|Writing, counting and timekeeping|Maya scribes combined writing, mathematics and intricate calendars. Ancient cities changed and sometimes declined. Maya peoples, languages and traditions continue today.

-260|Third century BCE|South Asia|Edicts of Ashoka|War remembered on stone|Ashoka’s edicts describe suffering after the conquest of Kalinga and express remorse. They are also political texts commissioned by the victorious ruler.

105|Early centuries CE|East Asia|History of paper|A writing surface travels|Chinese papermaking traditions spread through Eurasia. The familiar account crediting Cai Lun in 105 CE coexists with archaeological finds of earlier paper.

750|Eighth–thirteenth centuries|West Asia|Graeco-Arabic translation movement|Knowledge changes in translation|Translators working across Greek, Syriac and Arabic carried texts into new settings. Scholars corrected and extended them. Translation was itself intellectual work.

1000|c. 1000 CE|North Atlantic|L'Anse aux Meadows|An Atlantic crossing leaves traces|Norse structures in Newfoundland provide physical evidence of a transatlantic crossing. The continents were already home to Indigenous societies with deep histories.

1200|Medieval southern Africa|Southern Africa|Great Zimbabwe|Who built Great Zimbabwe?|Stone enclosures and trade goods document a major African urban centre. Colonial writers promoted foreign-builder stories despite archaeological evidence for local construction. Those claims reveal the politics of interpretation.

1324|1324–1325|West Africa|Mansa Musa|A pilgrimage connects cities|Musa’s journey from Mali to Mecca linked West African wealth and scholarship to wider networks. Contemporary reports describe the spectacle more fully than the labour sustaining it.

1347|Fourteenth century|Afro-Eurasia|Black Death|Plague and persecution|Ancient DNA links the pandemic to Yersinia pestis. Communities suffered enormous losses. False accusations that Jewish people caused the disease fuelled massacres.

1492|From 1492|Atlantic world|Columbian exchange|An ocean crossing transforms lives|Crops, animals and pathogens crossed oceans. Conquest, forced labour, dispossession and epidemics devastated Indigenous communities. Resistance and adaptation also shaped what followed.

1600|Seventeenth century and later|Pacific|History of Easter Island|Rapa Nui and the collapse debate|A popular account blamed deforestation for a pre-contact population crash. Ancient DNA research published in 2024 found no support for a severe seventeenth-century bottleneck in its model. Ecological change, population estimates and later slave raids are distinct questions.

1700|Early modern Atlantic|Atlantic world|Atlantic slave trade|Lives treated as cargo|Shipping and plantation records document the forced transport of millions of Africans. Totals are reconstructed across incomplete voyages. Testimony and histories of resistance restore experiences that ledgers conceal.

1791|1791–1804|Caribbean|Haitian Revolution|Enslaved people overthrow slavery|An uprising in Saint-Domingue became a revolution and led to independent Haiti. The victory changed the Atlantic world. Later demands for indemnity burdened generations.

1850|Nineteenth century|Australia|Australian frontier wars|Violence at the expanding frontier|Indigenous testimony, settler records and archaeology document dispossession, killings and resistance. Survivors’ accounts can preserve events omitted from official reports.

1915|From 1915|Ottoman Empire|Armenian genocide|Deportation and genocide|Authorities deported and killed Armenians on a mass scale. Survivor accounts, diplomatic reports and official records document the genocide. Disputes over precise totals do not erase the evidence.

1933|1933–1945|Europe|The Holocaust|Persecution becomes genocide|Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered six million Jews. Survivor testimony, perpetrator records and physical evidence establish the genocide. Historians continue to reconstruct individual lives and local decisions.

1945|August 1945|Japan|Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki|Two cities under atomic attack|The bombings killed civilians on a vast scale and left survivors with lasting injuries. Historians debate how the bombings and Soviet entry into the war affected Japan’s surrender.

1947|1947|South Asia|Partition of India|Borders drawn through homes|Partition and independence brought new states, mass displacement, killings and sexual violence. Oral histories preserve displacement at the scale of families. Death toll estimates vary.

1948|1948|Worldwide|Universal Declaration of Human Rights|A declaration after world war|Delegates adopted a shared statement of rights after the devastation of war and genocide. Its adoption and its enforcement are separate histories.

1960|Twentieth century|Africa|Decolonisation of Africa|Independence takes different paths|African movements built new states through negotiation, protest, strikes and armed struggle. Political independence did not automatically end colonial borders, debt or unequal economic relationships.

1980|1980|Worldwide|Eradication of smallpox|When smallpox transmission ended|Global certification followed vaccination campaigns and the tracing of outbreaks. Local health workers helped achieve a result no country could secure alone.

1994|1994|Central Africa|Rwandan genocide|Genocide in Rwanda|Extremists and their collaborators carried out genocide against the Tutsi. They also killed Hutu who opposed them. Survivor testimony and court records document neighbourhood-level choices.

2020|2020 onwards|Worldwide|COVID-19 pandemic|Living through a pandemic|Public records track deaths and responses unevenly across countries. Excess mortality, recorded deaths and personal testimony answer different questions about the same loss.
